01.text: Investigators, journalists and lawyers share one problem: too much evidence to read, and a result nobody can later prove was not changed.

05.text: Nothing counts until a person approves or declines it with a signature. Then the record is sealed, so anyone can check it later.

06.text: Four invented cases show how that helps.

07.text: One: a freight company pays a supplier, a consultant, a guarantor and a ship agent. Four desks, four clean files.

08.text: Kassar. Qassar. Khassar. Kasar. And on one licence, the name in Arabic.

09.text: Four spellings, two alphabets, one man. And one who is not him: a surveyor with the same name, born elsewhere.

10.text: AI read every page, the Arabic licence too, and pulled out each name, father and birth date. All six true links were found, each with the passage behind it. In a live test, the AI also set the surveyor aside on its own: born in another town.

11.text: A person declines the surveyor, with a reason, and signs each decision with a passkey on their own device.

12.text: The case closes on a conclusion, signed by a person and checked by a colleague: one man, under four names.

13.text: Two: a workshop burns down at night. The bookkeeper says she spent the evening at her sister's, thirty-four kilometres away.

15.text: Three: a flood video spreads as breaking news.

16.text: Four: a nurse boards a night bus and is never seen again.

17.text: Every decision is signed by a person, and the case is sealed. Here the first case's real package is checked in a browser, with nothing uploaded.

18.text: AI reads more than any team can. It sees what is buried in the mess. And a person signs every decision.

07b.text: Are they four people, or one man under four names? The desks hold fourteen sources and one thousand, four hundred and forty-five rows.

13b.text: Was she? There are forty-one statements to read.

14b.text: It describes the photograph from her phone, and writes down the voice note she sent.

15b.text: Is it new? The tip line holds thirty-six clips that look alike.

15c.text: The app compares their sound and ties the viral clip to a video posted two years earlier. It had been cropped and mirrored, so the picture no longer matched.

15d.text: Eight of nine reposts were tied this way; one muted copy is missed. A person signs that the clip is old.

16b.text: Where do you look? The bus company's logs run to several hundred lines.

16c.text: A supervisor's statement says when the driver was last seen. From that night, the app finds seventy-three days in which no log names him.

16d.text: The conclusion, signed and checked by a colleague: Aron Vesk is named in no log for the next seventy-three days; this is a lead to follow, not a finding about what he did.

14a.text: AI reads every paper itself. On this scanned exhibit sheet, it reads the page, then pulls out who was where, boxed where it is written.

14c.text: Then it flags what does not fit: those two exhibits place her at the workshop at twenty-one fifty-two and twenty-two oh seven, while she says she was away from six.

14d.text: A person checks both against her statement and signs: she was at the yard on Tanner's Row that evening, not in Brindle Cross from six.

04b.text: AI reads all of it, scans, photos, recordings and spreadsheets, and finds connections a person would miss, each pinned to the exact place it came from.
